Whether this represents appropriate functional separation or a structural gap in the board's ability to independently evaluate roadmap credibility and technical execution risk was a question that institutional investors and analysts had begun to pose with increasing frequency as Rigetti's market capitalization climbed above $8 billion.

## The Founder's Exit and Its Precedent

Chad Rigetti's departure ~~in March 2022~~ ==announced later in 2022== — described in company communications as a mutual agreement with the board — had no direct parallel among the company's closest public-market peers. At IonQ, the leading trapped-ion pure-play, founder Peter Chapman remained CEO through the same post-SPAC period, maintaining continuity of technical vision and founder equity alignment. At Rigetti, ~~the founder's exit preceded the SPAC closing by days, leaving the newly listed company without its primary technical identity figure at the precise moment it needed to establish credibility with public investors.~~ ==Chad Rigetti remained founder and CEO through the SPAC closing on March 2, 2022 and stepped down only later that year, leaving the newly listed company without its primary technical identity figure within months of needing to establish credibility with public investors.==

The separation agreement terms, as disclosed in the relevant 8-K filings, addressed standard provisions around equity vesting and non-competition obligations. Chad Rigetti, as of the 2026 leadership materials, held no board seat and carried no formal advisory designation. The IP continuity question — whether the departure of a Yale-trained physicist who had trained under superconducting qubit pioneer Michel Devoret created any research discontinuity — was never publicly adjudicated, and Rigetti's subsequent technical progress on fidelity and chiplet architecture suggested the engineering organization had absorbed and extended the founding scientific program without visible regression.

## Quanta's Strategic Footprint

Among the external influences on Rigetti's governance, Quanta Computer occupied a distinctive position following its [February 2025 collaboration announcement](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-appoints-dr-subodh-kulkarni-president-and) and subsequent $35 million equity investment at $11.59 per share, which closed in April 2025. At approximately $43 billion in annual revenue, Quanta was one of the world's largest electronics manufacturing services companies — the dominant producer of servers, notebooks, and networking hardware for hyperscale data center operators. Its decision to purchase Rigetti equity at what by mid-2026 had become a substantial discount to the prevailing share price reflected the appreciation trajectory that had characterized the stock during 2025.

The strategic collaboration agreement, filed as an [8-K on February 27, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001838359/000110465926023454/rgti-20251231x10k.htm), committed both parties to invest more than $100 million each over five years in superconducting quantum computing development. Quanta's board observation or designation rights under the agreement, if any, were not publicly detailed in the disclosed terms — meaning Quanta's influence on Rigetti's capital allocation and manufacturing strategy operated through commercial partnership channels rather than formal governance seats. What Quanta added to the oversight dynamic was nonetheless substantive: a manufacturing partner with direct experience scaling complex hardware systems from prototype to volume production, a distribution network reaching data center operators and national governments, and an institutional incentive to ensure that Rigetti's chiplet-based modular architecture eventually reached the form factor and reliability thresholds required for enterprise deployment.

The resulting leadership picture was of an organization that had deliberately assembled a post-founder management structure optimized for the commercialization phase of a deep-technology company — technically informed at the CTO level, commercially disciplined at the CEO and CFO level, and governed by a board whose primary expertise lay in scaling hardware businesses rather than advancing quantum physics. Whether that configuration proved sufficient for the transition from sub-$10 million annual revenue to the revenue base required to justify an $8.8 billion market capitalization remained the central governance question embedded in every forward projection Rigetti's leadership offered to the market.

chapters.title: Government Labs, National Quantum Centers, and Cloud Marketplace Users: Rigetti's Customer Ecosystem
chapters.body:
## A Government-Anchored Base

Rigetti Computing's customer roster at the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, remained concentrated in a handful of national quantum programs and defense laboratories — a customer profile that reflected both the maturity of the quantum computing market and the deliberate sequencing of Rigetti's commercial strategy. The company had identified fewer than ten named institutional hardware customers across its disclosed relationships, with sovereign and quasi-sovereign bodies accounting for the overwhelming majority of contract revenue. Understanding who those customers were, how they engaged with Rigetti's technology, and what their spending represented relative to total revenue was essential to evaluating whether Rigetti had built a durable commercial foundation or remained dependent on a narrow set of government patrons whose budget cycles and procurement timelines could shift without warning.

## The U.S. Federal Anchor: AFRL and the DOC Letter of Intent

The Air Force Research Laboratory stood as Rigetti's longest-tenured and most visible American government customer. AFRL's relationship with Rigetti had progressed beyond standard technology-development grants into hardware acquisition: the laboratory received ~~at least two deployments of the Novera 9-qubit on-premises QPU system~~ ==one of the two earliest disclosed Novera 9-qubit on-premises QPU deployments — the other going to Fermilab's Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center (SQMS) —== following the [Novera QPU Partner Program](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-yvxoh4p8fn7k) launch in April 2024. ~~These installations placed~~ ==This installation placed== an operational Rigetti processor inside a classified-adjacent defense research environment, validating that Rigetti's commercial hardware met the physical security and systems-integration requirements of military research programs — a certification with considerable downstream commercial value.

The more consequential federal development arrived in ~~March 2026~~ ==May 2026==, when Rigetti signed a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in research and development funding under national quantum computing programs. The LOI did not represent committed funding: letters of intent are non-binding statements of intent to negotiate, and ~~the conversion of that $100 million into actual contract revenue depended on Rigetti's ability to execute against technical milestones that had yet to be publicly specified~~ ==the conversion of that $100 million into committed funding depended on Rigetti's ability to execute against technical milestones that had yet to be publicly specified. The LOI also contemplated an equity stake for the Department of Commerce in exchange for the funding, meaning the prospective relationship was not cleanly non-dilutive==. Nonetheless, the DOC relationship materially elevated Rigetti's profile within the federal funding ecosystem at a moment when the U.S. government was accelerating investment in quantum-relevant supply chains.

## International Government Programs: The UK, India, and Israel

Beyond American federal customers, Rigetti had assembled a geographically diverse set of sovereign relationships that collectively represented the most commercially promising segment of its near-term hardware pipeline.

The United Kingdom's National Quantum Computing Centre in Didcot, Oxfordshire, hosted a Rigetti 36-qubit system — an installation that predated the Ankaa-class product line — and subsequently placed an Innovate UK-funded order for a 24-qubit Ankaa-class system. The NQCC relationship benefited from the broader context of the UK government's commitment to a quantum investment program; Rigetti's March 2026 announcement of plans to invest up to $100 million in the United Kingdom over the subsequent three to four years, culminating in a greater-than-1,000-qubit system, positioned the NQCC relationship as the seed of a much larger national infrastructure engagement.

India's Centre for Development of Advanced Computing represented the single largest hardware contract in Rigetti's disclosed history. C-DAC placed an approximately $8.4 million purchase order for a 108-qubit Cepheus-class on-premises quantum computing system, with delivery expected in the second half of 2026. The magnitude of this contract relative to Rigetti's financial scale deserves emphasis: Rigetti's full-year 2025 revenue was $7.1 million. The C-DAC order, if recognized in a single reporting period upon delivery, would exceed that entire annual figure by approximately 18 percent — a concentration that illustrates both the opportunity and the binary timing risk inherent in Rigetti's hardware-delivery revenue model. A single delayed shipment, a customs complication, or a technical acceptance-testing failure could materially shift a quarterly revenue figure by more than the company's entire prior-year revenue base.

Israel's national quantum computing center added a third sovereign relationship via a Novera QPU co-location alongside Quantum Machines' OPX1000 control system and NVIDIA Grace-Hopper servers — a configuration that demonstrated hybrid classical-quantum integration at the national infrastructure level. The Israeli deployment was notable not for its revenue scale (a 9-qubit Novera system represents an entry-level transaction) but for its systems-integration context: Rigetti's hardware operating alongside GPU-class classical compute in a national facility created a reference architecture that the company could cite in subsequent government procurement conversations globally.

## Asia-Pacific: Japan and the Quanta Channel

The Asia-Pacific footprint expanded during the latter part of 2025 when a Japanese research organization placed the first Novera QPU order from Japan, with delivery expected in April 2026. The Japanese customer's identity was not publicly disclosed, but the transaction extended Rigetti's on-premises hardware footprint into one of the world's most active national quantum programs — Japan's government had committed tens of billions of yen to quantum research through its Moonshot R&D program and related initiatives.

The more structurally significant Asia-Pacific development was the February 2025 strategic collaboration with Quanta Computer Inc., the Taiwan-headquartered server and notebook manufacturer that generated approximately $43 billion in annual revenue. Under the collaboration agreement, both parties committed to investing more than $100 million each over five years to develop superconducting quantum computing; Quanta separately acquired $35 million of Rigetti common stock at $11.59 per share, a transaction that closed in April 2025. The commercial logic was straightforward: Rigetti's ~~350-person~~ ==164-person== organization lacked the enterprise sales infrastructure to penetrate hyperscale data center operators, national government procurement offices, and defense contractors across Asia-Pacific, Europe, and the Americas simultaneously. Quanta's existing relationships with those exact customer categories — developed over decades of server and data center hardware supply — created a distribution pathway that Rigetti could not replicate organically. Whether those relationships would translate into quantum hardware orders remained unproven at the frozen snapshot date, but the partnership materially expanded the theoretical addressable customer base.

## Cloud Marketplace Access: AWS Braket and Microsoft Azure

Rigetti's QPU systems were available through Amazon Web Services Braket and Microsoft Azure, providing cloud-based access to academic researchers, quantum software developers, and enterprise exploratory teams without requiring on-premises hardware commitments. The cloud marketplace model served a fundamentally different customer profile than institutional hardware buyers: individual researchers, startup quantum software companies, and enterprise teams running early-stage algorithmic feasibility studies could access Rigetti's Ankaa-class and Cepheus-class systems at pay-per-use rates without capital expenditure.

The economics of cloud marketplace distribution carried structural trade-offs. Cloud providers typically retain 20 to 30 percent of listed compute revenue as marketplace fees, compressing Rigetti's realized yield on each QPU access transaction. On AWS Braket, Rigetti competed for developer attention alongside IonQ's trapped-ion systems and D-Wave's annealing-based offerings — two architecturally distinct approaches that served different algorithmic use cases. IonQ's higher gate fidelity (99.99 percent claimed accuracy) and D-Wave's established annealing customer base meant that Rigetti's transmon superconducting systems occupied a specific niche: high gate speed (tens of nanoseconds), a roadmap toward universal fault-tolerant computation, and fabrication scalability derived from semiconductor process techniques. Whether cloud marketplace QPU usage was generating measurable subscription or usage revenue in Rigetti's reported figures was not disclosed with granularity; the company's revenue disclosures aggregated contract and cloud revenue without segment-level breakdowns that would allow external analysis of cloud contribution.

## The Enterprise Gap

The most consequential ~~absence~~ ==thin layer== in Rigetti's customer map was ~~the one that did not appear: no disclosed commercial enterprise customer in financial services, pharmaceutical research, or materials science — the three sectors most frequently cited by quantum computing vendors and academic researchers as early beneficiaries of practical quantum advantage. No Fortune 500 company was named as a recurring cloud subscriber. No pharmaceutical firm had disclosed a quantum-chemistry simulation program running on Rigetti hardware. No financial institution had announced a portfolio optimization or risk-modeling engagement.~~ ==its commercial-enterprise tier. The FY2025 10-K named AWS, Standard Chartered Bank, and Moody's among Rigetti's partners and customers — anchoring the commercial roster with a global cloud hyperscaler, a major international bank, and a leading financial-data and analytics firm — but disclosure of those relationships was sparse: none was characterized with revenue, contract scale, or engagement-depth granularity that would allow external assessment of commercial significance. Beyond those three names, pharmaceutical research and materials science — two of the three sectors most frequently cited by quantum computing vendors and academic researchers as early beneficiaries of practical quantum advantage — had no named enterprise customer at all. No additional Fortune 500 company was named as a recurring cloud subscriber. No pharmaceutical firm had disclosed a quantum-chemistry simulation program running on Rigetti hardware. Beyond Standard Chartered, no other financial institution had announced a portfolio optimization or risk-modeling engagement.==

This gap could be interpreted two ways. The market-readiness interpretation held that commercial enterprises were rationally waiting for qubit counts, gate fidelities, and error-correction capabilities to reach thresholds that would yield demonstrable advantage over classical high-performance computing — thresholds that, at 108 qubits and sub-99.5 percent fidelity, had not yet been crossed. The sales-strategy interpretation held that Rigetti had deliberately prioritized government and research customers, where procurement processes were more patient, technology-development contracts were structurally available, and the company's relatively small sales organization could operate most efficiently. Both interpretations were consistent with the disclosed facts. What the ~~gap~~ ==thin layer== unambiguously confirmed was that Rigetti's commercial transformation — from government contractor to enterprise quantum service provider — remained, at the frozen snapshot date, ~~prospective rather than realized~~ ==in its early stages: a small set of named enterprise anchors had been disclosed, but not at a scale or recurrence that would constitute a realized commercial book of business==.

| Customer Segment | Key Relationships | Revenue Significance |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. Federal / Defense | AFRL (~~2× Novera~~ ==Novera==); DOC LOI (up to $100M) | Majority of historical contract base |
| International Government | UK NQCC (36-qubit + Ankaa order); India C-DAC ($8.4M); Israel QCC (Novera) | C-DAC alone exceeds FY2025 total revenue |
| Asia-Pacific Research | Japanese institution (Novera, April 2026 delivery); Quanta channel | Nascent; Quanta partnership unproven |
| Cloud Marketplace | AWS Braket; Microsoft Azure | Undisclosed; structurally modest vs. hardware |
| Commercial Enterprise | ~~None disclosed~~ ==AWS, Standard Chartered Bank, Moody's (per FY2025 10-K)== | ~~Material gap versus stated end-market thesis~~ ==Initial enterprise anchors disclosed; depth, revenue, and recurrence undisclosed== |

The customer ecosystem Rigetti had assembled by May 2026 was coherent as a proof-of-concept — sovereign buyers willing to pay for on-premises quantum hardware existed on four continents — but it was not yet a scalable commercial model. The revenue concentration in fewer than ten institutional relationships, the binary timing risk of multi-million-dollar hardware deliveries, and the ~~complete absence of enterprise commercial accounts~~ ==still-shallow disclosure of its enterprise commercial accounts== left Rigetti dependent on a customer base whose spending patterns were determined by government budget cycles, academic grant timelines, and national quantum strategy priorities rather than by commercial demand driven by measurable return on quantum investment.

chapters.title: Superconducting vs. Trapped-Ion vs. Annealing: Rigetti's Position in a Multi-Technology Quantum Race
chapters.body:
## Three Modalities, One Prize

Quantum computing entered its commercial phase without a dominant technology standard. Unlike classical computing's rapid convergence on silicon CMOS in the 1970s, the quantum hardware race of the mid-2020s featured at least four distinct physical implementations competing for the same long-term prize — practical quantum advantage over classical supercomputers — while disagreeing fundamentally on how to get there. For investors and enterprise buyers evaluating Rigetti Computing, the competitive map was not merely a list of companies but a technology-selection problem with multi-decade consequences: the winning modality would likely define the industry's structure, and the losers would find their capital bases eroded regardless of execution quality. Rigetti made an early, irreversible bet on superconducting transmon qubits. Whether that bet proves correct depends as much on physics as on management.

## Superconducting: A Three-Player Tier

Within the superconducting segment, the competitive hierarchy was pronounced. International Business Machines Corporation operated the most mature commercial quantum program by any measurable enterprise metric. By early 2026, IBM's quantum portfolio spanned the Eagle (127-qubit), Osprey (433-qubit), Condor (1,121-qubit), and Heron (133-qubit, with meaningfully improved error rates relative to Condor) generations — all accessible through IBM Cloud and backed by the IBM Quantum Network, a partner ecosystem comprising more than 270 organizations including Fortune 100 corporations, national laboratories, and leading research universities. IBM's fabrication infrastructure at Albany NanoTech, combined with decades of semiconductor process expertise, Watson brand equity, and a global enterprise sales force, positioned it as the default choice for large organizations making exploratory quantum investments. Rigetti did not compete with IBM for the enterprise customer that wanted a vendor-managed relationship with an established technology brand; it competed in the space that IBM's integrated, proprietary stack did not fully serve — independent developers, cloud-native research teams, and government programs that valued open access over ecosystem lock-in.

Google Quantum AI represented a different kind of competitive pressure. In December 2024, Google announced that its Willow superconducting chip had performed a computation in five minutes that would require a classical supercomputer approximately 10^25 years to replicate — a benchmark that, while carefully scoped to a specific sampling problem rather than a commercially relevant workload, reset the narrative baseline for what superconducting hardware could demonstrate. Google's quantum program remained research-first and was not commercially offered as a cloud service in any form comparable to Rigetti's QCS or IBM Cloud. Enterprise buyers could not purchase time on Willow. What Google's announcements created, instead, was a recurring investor expectation problem: each major Google milestone risked triggering the question of whether Rigetti's roadmap remained differentiated, even when the two companies were not competing for the same contracts. The narrative risk was real even where the commercial competition was not.

Rigetti's position in this tier was defined by what it was not. It was not IBM's scale, not Google's research prestige. Its differentiation rested on three structural attributes: independence from a cloud provider's proprietary ecosystem, open cloud access through QCS, AWS Braket, and Microsoft Azure simultaneously, and — most distinctively — full-stack vertical integration through Fab-1.

## Trapped-Ion: The Fidelity Benchmark

The more direct commercial contest was with the trapped-ion companies, particularly IonQ. The technology vectors diverged sharply on the metrics that enterprise customers cited in vendor evaluations.

| Metric | Rigetti (superconducting) | IonQ (trapped-ion) |
|---|---|---|
| Two-qubit gate fidelity | ~~99.5% (Cepheus GA) / 99.9% (prototype)~~ ==99.1% median (Cepheus-1-108Q at April 2026 GA); 99.5% later-2026 target; 99.9% (prototype)== | 99.99% (claimed) |
| Gate speed | ~28 nanoseconds | ~100–1,000 microseconds |
| Gate speed advantage | ~10,000× faster than trapped-ion | Baseline |
| Deployed qubit count | 108 (Cepheus-1) | Smaller ion trap systems; different architecture |
| FY2025 revenue | $7.1 million | $130 million |
| Cash position (approx.) | $569 million (March 31, 2026) | Public filings vary |
| Cloud availability | QCS, AWS Braket, Azure | AWS Braket, Azure, Google Cloud |

IonQ's revenue advantage was not marginal — it was categorical. At $130 million in FY2025 revenue against Rigetti's $7.1 million, IonQ had demonstrated an ability to convert enterprise and government interest into contracted revenue at a scale Rigetti had not approached. IonQ's partnerships with AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud gave it a distribution breadth comparable to Rigetti's cloud presence, and its 99.99% claimed gate fidelity consistently featured in enterprise sales materials as a differentiator over superconducting alternatives.

The superconducting counterargument was speed. Trapped-ion gate operations measured in microseconds versus Rigetti's 28-nanosecond gate time represented a roughly 10,000x throughput differential — and while current circuit depths remained shallow enough that this gap had limited practical impact, the trajectory toward error-corrected computation requiring millions of gate operations per logical computation would, in Rigetti's framing, make gate speed a decisive production constraint. Faster gates also meant less coherence-time consumption per operation, a relevant efficiency in systems where decoherence remained the primary engineering bottleneck.

Quantinuum, the private trapped-ion company formed from Honeywell Quantum Solutions and Cambridge Quantum Computing, did not publish revenue figures. Backed by Honeywell — a company with deep enterprise relationships across aerospace, defense, and industrial sectors — Quantinuum operated the H2 trapped-ion system and had publicly claimed quantum volume leadership at various points in its roadmap cycle. Its enterprise-facing narrative emphasized Honeywell's existing customer relationships as a distribution channel that no pure-play startup could replicate. Were Quantinuum to pursue a public market listing, institutional capital currently allocated to RGTI could face reallocation pressure toward a better-capitalized, better-revenues trapped-ion vehicle. As of the frozen snapshot, no definitive Quantinuum IPO timeline had been publicly announced, but the possibility hung over sector sentiment.

## Alternative Modalities: Annealing and Long-Dated Photonics

D-Wave Quantum (NASDAQ: QBTS) operated the quantum annealing segment largely in isolation from the gate-based competition. Annealing processors were purpose-built for combinatorial optimization problems — logistics routing, scheduling, molecular simulation variants — rather than universal quantum computation. D-Wave's commercial path was therefore narrower by design, and the company's near-term revenue model reflected it. For enterprise buyers with specific optimization workloads, D-Wave represented an immediately deployable option; for those seeking general-purpose quantum processing, it did not compete with Rigetti.

PsiQuantum, the photonic quantum computing company backed by SoftBank, Microsoft, and others, occupied an unusual position: a company with an exceptionally long capital horizon, pursuing fault-tolerant photonic computation at the million-qubit scale but without any deployed commercial system as of mid-2026. PsiQuantum's thesis was that photonic qubits could ultimately be manufactured at semiconductor wafer scale, but its timeline to practical relevance extended years beyond any period relevant to Rigetti's current competitive assessment. QuEra Computing and Atom Computing, both operating neutral-atom platforms, similarly remained pre-commercial research programs rather than active competitors for enterprise contract revenue.

## Vertical Integration: Moat and Burden

The most structurally distinctive feature of Rigetti's competitive position was Fab-1. No other publicly traded pure-play quantum company operated a proprietary superconducting qubit fabrication facility. IBM maintained fabrication capability at Albany NanoTech, but as part of a broader research infrastructure rather than a standalone commercial moat. IonQ and Quantinuum did not fabricate chips at all — their trapped-ion systems used atomic physics rather than lithographic process steps. Rigetti's ownership of the full manufacturing stack — from qubit geometry design through coupler fabrication, packaging, and integration into dilution refrigerator systems — created process differentiation that was difficult to replicate through contractual relationships with third-party semiconductor fabs, and generated IP in qubit design and process chemistry that was not easily reverse-engineered.

The burden was equally structural. Fab-1 required continuous capital expenditure for equipment, process chemistry, and engineering staffing. Every design iteration on a new QPU generation consumed cleanroom time, consumables, and engineering cycles. The $569 million cash position as of March 31, 2026, provided the balance sheet depth to sustain this investment across multiple development cycles — but the capital requirement of vertical integration created a fixed-cost floor that a competitor outsourcing its fabrication did not bear.

The competitive calculus, in synthesis, was that Rigetti had accepted the capital burden of vertical integration in exchange for the strategic option of proprietary process control — a trade that would prove correct if the superconducting roadmap converged toward fault tolerance faster than trapped-ion or photonic alternatives, and incorrect if an architecturally different modality captured the practical-advantage threshold first.

chapters.title: Timeline of Technical Milestones and Forward Catalysts: From Ankaa-2 to the 1,000-Qubit UK System
chapters.body:
## A Twenty-Eight-Month Chronicle of Execution

Rigetti Computing entered 2024 with a credibility deficit that its engineering team had been quietly closing. In January of that year, the company announced general availability of Ankaa-2, an 84-qubit system reporting 98% median two-qubit gate fidelity — a 2.5× performance improvement over the prior generation and the company's first system to cross the threshold typically associated with near-term algorithmic utility. Ankaa-2 subsequently appeared on both Amazon Web Services Braket and Microsoft Azure, extending Rigetti's cloud reach without additional distribution infrastructure. The announcement was a technical milestone, not a revenue event: cloud-access subscriptions remained marginal, and the fidelity figure, while meaningful in the physics literature, did not yet translate to commercially differentiated quantum advantage.

The following spring brought a more commercially significant development. In April 2024, Rigetti launched the [Novera QPU Partner Program](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024), formally commercializing its 9-qubit on-premises processor as a deployable research instrument. The program generated two early-mover transactions: ~~a second Novera unit to the Air Force Research Laboratory, deepening a government relationship that had existed since the company's early contract phase~~ ==a Novera unit to the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab, building on the earlier Air Force Research Laboratory placement that had anchored Rigetti's government research relationships==, and a co-location at Israel's national quantum computing center alongside NVIDIA Grace-Hopper servers and Quantum Machines' OPX1000 control system. Neither order was large enough to register as a material revenue item, but the partner program structure established the contractual and logistical framework for subsequent hardware deployments — a scaffolding that would prove useful when larger orders arrived.

The year closed with another fidelity step-change. In December 2024, Rigetti launched Ankaa-3, maintaining the 84-qubit count but achieving 99.0% median iSWAP gate fidelity and 99.5% with fSim gates. The progression from Ankaa-2 to Ankaa-3 in twelve months — moving the key fidelity metric from 98% to 99.5% — illustrated that Rigetti's in-house Fab-1 process was advancing on a measurable, if not linear, schedule.

## Partnership, Capital, and the First Large Hardware Order

The first quarter of 2025 marked a pivot from technical demonstration toward commercial architecture. On February 27, 2025, Rigetti announced a strategic collaboration with Quanta Computer Inc., the Taiwanese server and notebook manufacturer reporting approximately $43 billion in annual revenue. Under the agreement, both parties committed to investing more than $100 million each over five years in superconducting quantum computing development. Quanta separately agreed to invest $35 million in Rigetti common stock at $11.59 per share; that transaction closed in April 2025 following regulatory clearance. The Quanta relationship mattered for a reason beyond its capital contribution: Quanta's global distribution infrastructure — serving hyperscale data centers, enterprise IT buyers, and government technology programs — represented a go-to-market channel that Rigetti could not replicate organically at its current scale.

The company simultaneously raised $350 million in gross proceeds through its at-the-market equity offering during 2025, producing a year-end cash balance of $589.8 million against zero long-term debt. That capital position, accumulated through successive dilutive equity issuances rather than operations, provided what management described as a multi-year operational runway — though at the cost of a 47.6% year-over-year increase in shares outstanding to ~~332.4 million~~ ==332.3 million==.

Later in 2025, two hardware orders validated the on-premises deployment thesis. In late 2025, a Japanese research institution placed the first Novera QPU order from Japan, with delivery expected in April 2026 — evidence that Rigetti's Asia-Pacific commercial reach, seeded by the Sydney office, was beginning to generate transactions. More consequentially, India's Centre for Development of Advanced Computing placed an approximately $8.4 million purchase order for a 108-qubit Cepheus-class on-premises system — the company's largest single hardware contract to date and its first major emerging-market government engagement. A prototype system during the same period demonstrated 99.9% two-qubit gate fidelity at 28-nanosecond gate speed, representing a threshold that researchers in the field associate with near-term quantum error correction experiments.

## ~~March 2026~~ ==Spring 2026==: A Compressed News Cycle

~~Within a single month~~ ==Across the spring of 2026==, Rigetti's external environment shifted materially. The March 4, 2026 release of Q4 and full-year 2025 results — FY2025 revenue of $7.1 million, down from $10.8 million the prior year due to contract-milestone timing — would have been the dominant story in isolation. But two subsequent announcements restructured the narrative. ~~Rigetti signed a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in R&D funding under national quantum computing programs, positioning the company as a recipient in the broader CHIPS Act quantum allocation framework.~~ ==On May 21, 2026, Rigetti signed a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in R&D funding under national quantum computing programs, with terms contemplating an equity stake for the Department alongside the cash commitment.== ~~Simultaneously, Rigetti announced plans to invest up to $100 million in the United Kingdom over three to four years~~ ==Rigetti also announced plans to invest up to $100 million of its own capital in the United Kingdom over three to four years==, with the centrepiece a greater-than-1,000-qubit quantum system — the company's first major facility outside the United States — building upon the existing 36-qubit Ankaa-class deployment at the National Quantum Computing Centre in Didcot, Oxfordshire. ~~The Cepheus-1-108Q entered general availability in Q1 2026.~~ ==Rigetti announced general availability of the Cepheus-1-108Q on April 7, 2026.==

On May 11, 2026, Q1 2026 earnings confirmed the first credible inflection: revenue of $4.4 million represented 193% year-over-year growth, ~~driven by partial recognition of Novera QPU shipment milestones and early Cepheus-class deliveries~~ ==driven primarily by higher Novera system and related product sales, including a shipment to the University of Saskatchewan==.

## The Catalyst Stack: Five Risk-Adjusted Vectors

As of May 23, 2026, Rigetti's forward narrative resolves into a defined set of catalysts, each carrying asymmetric risk.

| Catalyst | Expected Timing | Revenue Type | Key Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| C-DAC 108-qubit delivery | H2 2026 | ~$8.4M hardware | Hardware slippage; quantum systems have historically shipped late |
| DOC LOI → formal grant conversion | H2 2026 – 2027 | ~~Up to $100M non-dilutive~~ ==Up to $100M with equity component== | CHIPS Act disbursements have been slower than announced timelines |
| UK site selection and initial deployment | 2027–2029 | Capital investment phase | LOI is non-binding; geopolitical or budget reallocations can alter commitments |
| Quanta first joint commercial customer | 2026–2027 | Strategic validation | Partnership is collaboration-stage; no joint customer has been disclosed |
| Next-generation system announcement (beyond 108Q) | 2026–2027 | Technical roadmap signal | Engineering milestones in quantum hardware are difficult to project precisely |
| Enterprise/hyperscale cloud contract | Unknown | Recurring subscription | ~~No non-government commercial customer has been publicly named~~ ==FY2025 10-K names AWS, Standard Chartered Bank, and Moody's among partners and customers, but no material commercial revenue contribution has been separately disclosed== |

The C-DAC delivery is the nearest-term revenue catalyst with a fixed contract value and a disclosed timeline. Hardware delivery in quantum computing has historically slipped — superconducting systems require precision cryogenic packaging, custom control electronics, and site qualification at the receiving institution — and a six-to-twelve-month schedule compression risk is plausible. The DOC LOI conversion from letter of intent to executed grant carries structural delay risk: the Department of Energy's quantum program disbursements and the CHIPS Act semiconductor grants both demonstrated multi-quarter gaps between announcement and funding release.

The UK commitment warrants particular scrutiny. The $100 million figure is a stated investment plan tied to a letter of intent, not a signed contract. The 1,000-qubit system it contemplates represents a four-to-eight-fold increase over Rigetti's current largest deployed system, requiring fabrication process advances — chiplet interconnect yield, coherence-time preservation at scale — that have not yet been demonstrated at that qubit count by any superconducting competitor. If the underlying engineering trajectory fails to deliver sufficient fidelity at scale, the UK deployment timeline will shift regardless of ~~government funding availability~~ ==Rigetti's planned capital commitments==.

The most consequential unresolved variable is whether the Quanta partnership produces a disclosed enterprise or hyperscale cloud customer at material revenue scale. ~~Every other milestone — government contracts, fidelity demonstrations, national quantum program participation — is consistent with a company executing a government-funded research roadmap. A named commercial customer outside government would represent a qualitative shift in the thesis, confirming that the quantum computing market is generating demand at commercially meaningful price points from buyers not subsidised by national security or industrial policy objectives. Through May 2026, that evidence had not arrived.~~ ==The FY2025 10-K names AWS, Standard Chartered Bank, and Moody's among partners and customers, alongside the Ankaa-2 distribution presence on AWS Braket and Microsoft Azure, but the revenue contribution from these commercial relationships is not separately disclosed and is presumed modest relative to government and research-institution contracts. A materially larger commercial engagement — particularly one routed through Quanta's distribution channel — would mark the qualitative shift in the thesis, confirming that the quantum computing market is generating demand at commercially meaningful price points from buyers not subsidised by national security or industrial policy objectives. Through May 2026, that evidence had not arrived at scale.==

chapters.title: Fab-1, Patent Portfolio, and the Trade-Secret Moat: Rigetti's Intellectual Property Framework
chapters.body:
## A Cleanroom as a Competitive Moat

Rigetti Computing's intellectual property strategy departs from the conventional playbook of semiconductor and software firms. Rather than anchoring its competitive position in a large patent thicket, Rigetti has built a layered moat that combines a carefully defended formal patent estate with an even more formidable body of trade secrets embedded in the physical processes of Fab-1, its Fremont cleanroom. Understanding the distinction between what Rigetti has chosen to patent, what it has chosen to keep secret, and what U.S. and foreign governments now have a conditional right to access is essential to evaluating the durability of the company's technological lead.

## The Patent Estate and the IPR Test

The centerpiece of Rigetti's published patent portfolio is [U.S. Patent No. 9,836,699](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9836699B1/), titled "Microwave Integrated Quantum Circuits With Interposer," assigned to Rigetti & Co, LLC, the operating subsidiary. The patent covers a foundational architecture for connecting superconducting quantum processor chips to classical control electronics — specifically, the use of an interposer substrate to route microwave signals between qubits and their associated control lines without the parasitic interference that degrades coherence times. In superconducting systems, where qubit lifetimes are measured in microseconds and signal noise is the adversary of gate fidelity, the geometry of that interface is not a detail; it is the product.

The patent's significance was tested and substantially confirmed when Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, Rigetti's patent counsel, successfully defended it against two Inter Partes Review (IPR) petitions before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board. IPR proceedings — adversarial reexaminations initiated by parties seeking to invalidate a patent — are widely regarded as the most rigorous post-grant validity test in U.S. patent law. Surviving two separate IPR challenges establishes not merely that the claims were initially granted, but that they withstood concentrated adversarial scrutiny with full prior-art searches. The practical implication is that the '699 patent's claims are now substantially more difficult to challenge in future litigation, materially enhancing their defensive and licensing value. A search of Rigetti & Co, LLC assignments on Justia Patents reveals additional issued patents covering aspects of qubit control electronics, signal routing, and superconducting circuit design, indicating a portfolio of meaningful breadth across the signal-delivery stack — though the precise qubit geometry and junction-formation chemistry that determine processor performance are largely absent from the published claims for reasons discussed below.

## Fab-1 and the Trade-Secret Architecture

The most commercially critical elements of Rigetti's process knowledge cannot be fully protected by patent. A patent requires public disclosure; for a superconducting quantum chip, the parameters that matter most — the precise geometry of the Josephson junctions that define qubit frequency, the anneal cycles and oxidation conditions that set junction resistance uniformity, the coupler design and tunable coupling strengths, the packaging protocols that maintain cryogenic performance after chip bonding — are each individually discoverable through reverse engineering but are, collectively, extraordinarily difficult to replicate without the tacit knowledge accumulated through years of iterative fabrication runs.

This creates a trade-secret moat that is structurally different from a patent portfolio. Patents are public, enforceable, and licensable. Trade secrets embedded in Fab-1's process flows are opaque to competitors but also illiquid: Rigetti cannot easily license a fabrication recipe that it has never fully codified in a transferable form, and the moat's value depends entirely on the physical continuity of the Fremont facility and the institutional memory of the engineers who run it. The Cepheus-1 chiplet architecture — in which multiple smaller dies are bonded into a 108-qubit module — further deepens this complexity. Each chiplet boundary introduces a new set of process variables for inter-die connectivity, coupler placement, and signal integrity, and the company's demonstrated ability to achieve ~~99.5%~~ ==99.1%== median ~~fSim~~ ==two-qubit== gate fidelity across bonded chiplets ==at Cepheus-1-108Q general availability, with 99.5% set as a later-2026 target,== reflects process discipline that is almost entirely invisible to external observers.

## R&D Spending and the Fidelity Dividend

Against FY2025 revenue of $7.1 million and a non-GAAP operating loss of $50.5 million, research and development constitutes the overwhelmingly dominant line item in Rigetti's cost structure. SEC 10-K disclosures confirm that R&D expenditure has consistently exceeded revenue by a factor of four or more in recent fiscal years, reflecting the capital intensity of sustaining a dedicated quantum fabrication facility and a full-time hardware engineering organization. The return on that expenditure is visible in the fidelity progression: from sub-90% two-qubit gate fidelity in 2021 to 99.0% median iSWAP fidelity on Ankaa-3 in December 2024, to ~~99.5% median fSim fidelity on Cepheus-1 in Q1 2026~~ ==99.1% current median two-qubit gate fidelity at Cepheus-1-108Q general availability on April 7, 2026 (with 99.5% set as a later-2026 target)==, to a prototype system demonstrating 99.9% two-qubit gate fidelity at 28-nanosecond gate speed. Each increment in fidelity is not a linear improvement in output quality — it is an exponential compression of logical error rates, and the 99.9% threshold on the prototype is the figure that quantum error correction theorists conventionally cite as the lower bound for practical surface-code implementation. R&D productivity, measured in fidelity points per dollar spent, has accelerated materially since Kulkarni restructured the engineering organization in 2023.

## The Quanta Collaboration and Joint IP Ownership

The February 2025 strategic collaboration agreement with Quanta Computer introduces a more complex IP governance layer. [Per the 8-K filed with the SEC on February 27, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=RGTI&type=8-K), the collaboration involves joint development of superconducting quantum computing systems — combining Rigetti's QPU fabrication and software stack with Quanta's systems integration, manufacturing infrastructure, and global distribution. The critical IP demarcation, consistent with the disclosure, is that Rigetti retains sole ownership of QPU fabrication intellectual property: qubit design, chip architecture, and the Fab-1 process know-how remain exclusively Rigetti's. Jointly developed innovations — principally in system integration, cryogenic packaging for commercial deployment, and classical-quantum interface hardware — are governed by co-development IP provisions under which ownership depends on the contribution structure of each deliverable. This arrangement protects Rigetti's core fabrication moat while allowing Quanta to acquire rights in the systems integration layer it is actually contributing to — an economically rational division that avoids the scenario where a $43 billion OEM partner accumulates rights over the technology it did not develop.

## DOC Funding and March-In Rights

The ~~March~~ ==May== 2026 letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in R&D funding carries significant IP implications that have not been fully priced into market commentary. Federal research grants awarded under the Bayh-Dole Act framework — which governs IP rights in federally funded inventions — require recipients to grant the government a royalty-free license to any invention developed with federal funds, and preserve the government's "march-in" rights to require licensing to third parties if the recipient fails to commercialize the invention on a sufficient timeline or if the government determines action is necessary to address a public health or safety need. If the DOC LOI converts to a formal grant agreement, any QPU architectures or fabrication processes developed with those funds would be subject to these provisions — a meaningful qualification on the exclusivity of Rigetti's IP in those specific domains. ==The LOI also contemplates an equity stake for the Department, so the capital cannot be characterized as cleanly non-dilutive.== The CHIPS Act provisions applied to semiconductor fabricators offer a structural analogy: TSMC and Samsung accepted similar domestic manufacturing conditions and government licensing rights as a condition of federal funding, accepting IP constraints in exchange for capital access that accelerated facility expansion. For Rigetti, the $100 million in potential DOC funding likely exceeds the licensing risk for most commercially realistic scenarios, particularly given that march-in rights have been exercised by the federal government only rarely in the Bayh-Dole era. The more immediate IP obligation is the domestic manufacturing condition: qualifying for DOC quantum funding will almost certainly require that relevant fabrication activities remain at Fab-1 in Fremont, reinforcing rather than undermining the trade-secret moat's geographic concentration.

chapters.title: Six Material Risks: Pre-Commercial Revenue, Technology Competition, Dilution, Hardware Scale-Up, Geopolitical Dependencies, and Regulatory Uncertainty
chapters.body:
## Risk One: A Revenue Model That Has Never Covered Its Costs

Rigetti Computing has never reported an operating profit, and the gap between its commercial receipts and its cash consumption remained vast as of the frozen window. [Full-year 2025 revenue of $7.1 million](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-yvxoh4p8fn7k) — a sequential decline from $10.8 million in FY2024 and $12.0 million in FY2023 — reflected the lumpy, milestone-gated nature of government technology-development contracts rather than any deterioration in customer relationships. The non-GAAP operating loss for FY2025 ran to $50.5 million, implying a cash burn rate of roughly $12–15 million per quarter.

The company's $569.0 million in cash and investments as of March 31, 2026 provides a substantial buffer — at the FY2025 burn rate, a theoretical runway ~~exceeding four years~~ ==approaching a decade== — but that calculation is static and almost certainly optimistic. Scaling hardware from 108 qubits toward the 1,000-plus-qubit threshold, building out UK facilities, and funding the Quanta Computer collaboration will accelerate spending materially. A simple path-to-breakeven model is instructive: at gross margins of 40 percent (aspirational for a hardware-plus-cloud hybrid business), Rigetti would need annual revenue of approximately $125 million to cover a $50 million operating cost base — roughly 18 times its FY2025 figure. At the Q1 2026 annualized run rate of approximately $17.6 million, the company remains a full order of magnitude away. Revenue concentration compounds the risk: every dollar of FY2025 revenue derived from government and institutional contracts whose timing is outside management's control.

## Risk Two: Better-Capitalized Competitors Are Not Standing Still

Rigetti's three most formidable adversaries — IBM, Google, and IonQ — each presented distinct and escalating competitive threats during the review period.

IBM's quantum hardware program, embedded within a $60-billion-plus enterprise technology business, continued deploying superconducting systems through its IBM Quantum Network at a scale of engineering resources Rigetti cannot match. Google's research division published the Willow chip results in late 2024, demonstrating error-correction below threshold — a milestone Rigetti's own systems had not yet publicly replicated at comparable qubit counts. IonQ, the leading trapped-ion pure-play, reported [FY2025 revenue of $130 million](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-yvxoh4p8fn7k) — more than eighteen times Rigetti's — and claimed 99.99% two-qubit gate accuracy, exceeding Rigetti's best publicly demonstrated figure of 99.9% on a prototype system.

| Competitor | Technology | FY2025 Revenue | Key Claim |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rigetti Computing | Superconducting (transmon) | $7.1M | 99.9% two-qubit fidelity (prototype) |
| IonQ | Trapped-ion | $130M | 99.99% gate accuracy |
| IBM Quantum | Superconducting | Not ring-fenced | Enterprise deployment at scale |
| Google Quantum AI | Superconducting | Not ring-fenced | Willow below-threshold error correction |
| Quantinuum | Trapped-ion (private) | Not disclosed | Enterprise contracts, H-series systems |

Rigetti's defenders point to structural differentiation: the company's in-house Fab-1 foundry gives it process control that IBM analogues and IonQ's ion-trap supply chain cannot replicate, and its open-cloud positioning across AWS Braket and Azure broadens developer access beyond IBM's proprietary Quantum Network. The Quanta Computer partnership adds manufacturing and distribution leverage unavailable to any pure-play competitor. These are genuine advantages. The harder question is whether they are durable. IBM could open its superconducting processes to external cloud access more aggressively; Google has the capital to vertically integrate at any point; IonQ's revenue lead means it can fund algorithm development and enterprise sales at a pace Rigetti has not matched. Vertical integration is a moat only insofar as it generates compounding fidelity improvements faster than well-resourced alternatives — and the Willow milestone suggested that gap was narrowing from both directions.

## Risk Three: Relentless Share-Count Expansion

The dilution trajectory was among the most concrete financial risks disclosed in Rigetti's filings. Shares outstanding grew from approximately 225 million in early 2025 to [~~332.4~~ ==332.3== million by Q1 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001838359/000110465926023454/rgti-20251231x10k.htm) — a 47.6% increase in twelve months, driven primarily by the $350 million at-the-market equity program completed during 2025. The ATM program remained active as of the frozen window, meaning further issuance was a disclosed possibility rather than a theoretical one.

The SPAC transaction introduced a second dilution vector that continues to shadow the balance sheet: derivative warrant ~~and earn-out~~ liabilities whose fair-value movements dominated GAAP earnings in both directions. In Q1 2026, a ~~$62.1~~ ==$53.7== million non-cash gain on derivative warrant liabilities helped produce a GAAP net income of $33.1 million while the underlying operating business burned $14.7 million on a non-GAAP basis. Investors who read only the headline number received a materially misleading picture. Warrant exercises convert to common shares; earn-out liabilities are contingent on price thresholds that, given RGTI's 1,555% market-cap appreciation during 2025, were approaching or breaching. Each conversion adds to share count without adding a dollar of operational consideration.

At ~~332.4~~ ==332.3== million diluted shares and a market capitalization of approximately $8.79 billion as of May 22, 2026, Rigetti traded at a revenue multiple exceeding 400 times trailing twelve-month revenue — a valuation that prices in successful commercialization outcomes many years into the future. Per-share dilution of nearly 48% in a single year, if continued at any fraction of that pace, would reduce each existing shareholder's claim on those future outcomes proportionally even if the business itself progressed.

## Risk Four: The Chiplet Roadmap to 1,000 Qubits Is Unproven

Rigetti's chosen path to large-scale quantum computing — a modular chiplet architecture in which smaller processor tiles are interconnected to build higher qubit counts — had not been demonstrated beyond 108 qubits as of the frozen window. The Cepheus-1-108Q system, launched into general availability ~~in Q1 2026~~ ==in April 2026==, was the architectural proof of concept, but scaling from 108 to 1,000-plus qubits introduces compounding engineering challenges that grow non-linearly with system size.

Three technical variables are particularly sensitive to scale. Coherence times — the window during which a qubit retains its quantum state — degrade under the thermal and electromagnetic crosstalk conditions generated by denser chip arrays. Inter-chip connectivity fidelity, which governs how reliably quantum states can be transferred between chiplets, has not been publicly benchmarked at the multi-tile configurations required for 1,000 qubits. And cryogenic system complexity — specifically, the dilution refrigerators that must maintain processor temperatures near absolute zero — scales in cost, footprint, and failure probability as chip counts grow. Rigetti's UK commitment to deploy a greater-than-1,000-qubit system within three to four years carries a timeline that, given where the chiplet architecture stood at the frozen window, must be described as aspirational rather than engineered.

## Risk Five: Geopolitical and Supply Chain Concentration

Rigetti's global expansion strategy simultaneously increased its exposure to geopolitical risk vectors. The Quanta Computer partnership — the company's most consequential commercial relationship — involves a [Taiwan-based manufacturer](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001838359/000110465926023454/rgti-20251231x10k.htm) whose operations are subject to cross-strait tension risk and whose investments in U.S. technology companies attract Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States scrutiny. The $35 million Quanta equity investment cleared regulatory review in April 2025, but any future deepening of the relationship — joint manufacturing facilities, co-ownership of IP, or data-center deployments in Asia involving Rigetti systems — could trigger additional CFIUS or Department of Commerce review.

Fabrication inputs introduce a second dependency layer. The aluminum circuits, silicon substrates, and specialized cryogenic components used in superconducting QPU production are sourced from a small number of global suppliers, several of whom are subject to the same semiconductor supply chain constraints that disrupted conventional chip manufacturing during 2021–2023. Rigetti's Fab-1 in Fremont provides process control but does not eliminate upstream materials risk. Separately, both the DOC letter of intent for up to $100 million in R&D funding ==(which contemplated an equity stake for the Department, making the award dilutive rather than a clean grant)== and ~~the UK's commitment to host~~ ==Rigetti's announced intention to invest up to $100 million in the UK to host== a 1,000-plus-qubit facility are contingent on policy continuity across governments that could shift priorities — particularly given U.S. federal budget compression debates and the UK's evolving post-Brexit industrial strategy.

## Risk Six: Export Controls in an Unresolved Regulatory Landscape

Quantum computing hardware sits in one of the most actively contested jurisdictions of U.S. export control law. The Export Administration Regulations and the Commerce Control List were, as of the frozen window, being revised specifically to address quantum processing units, cryogenic control systems, and quantum software tools with potential dual-use applications. Rigetti's international deployment portfolio — the C-DAC 108-qubit contract in India, the Novera QPU co-located at Israel's national quantum computing center, and the anticipated Quanta-brokered distribution into Asian markets — each carried distinct export license exposure that the company had not fully disclosed in public filings.

The C-DAC delivery, scheduled for the second half of 2026, required navigating both U.S. export licensing for advanced quantum hardware and India's own technology procurement regulations. The Israeli co-location, while in a treaty-aligned jurisdiction, involved hardware at a national defense-adjacent facility alongside NVIDIA Grace-Hopper servers — a configuration that combined controlled dual-use technologies in ways regulators were still adjudicating. DOC and the National Security Agency were both actively engaged in quantum technology export control framework updates as of the frozen window, meaning the compliance environment into which Rigetti planned its international expansion was materially incomplete. A single adverse licensing determination could delay or void a hardware contract; a broader reclassification of superconducting QPUs under more restrictive control categories could structurally impair the company's international revenue thesis before it had generated meaningful scale.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The Twelve-Month Window

Rigetti Computing enters the twelve months beginning late May 2026 in a structurally different condition than it occupied twelve months prior. The company has $569.0 million in cash and investments and zero debt as of March 31, 2026. It has posted its first quarter of triple-digit revenue growth. It holds a signed letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $100 million in R&D funding. And it has a live customer deployment on order — the $8.4 million C-DAC 108-qubit Cepheus-class system destined for India — that will serve as the single largest revenue recognition event in Rigetti's eleven-year history if it delivers on schedule. The question the next twelve months will answer is whether Q1 2026's $4.4 million print was a one-quarter inflection or the first step of a durable hardware-delivery ramp.

## The Catalyst Calendar

The cadence of events is unusually compressible. Rigetti reports roughly sixty to seventy days after quarter-end — Q1 2026 results arrived May 11, 2026 — establishing a rhythm of four earnings windows before the frozen snapshot's twelve-month anniversary.

**Q2 2026 earnings (expected early August 2026)** will carry two specific line items to watch: partial milestone revenue from the C-DAC contract, which is structured as a hardware delivery agreement with milestone-linked payments rather than a lump-sum recognition, and any incremental Novera QPU orders from the growing Asia-Pacific pipeline. The Japanese research institution that placed its first Novera order in late 2025 — with delivery originally expected April 2026 — should appear as recognized revenue in either Q1 or Q2 2026 depending on acceptance timing. If the Quanta Computer collaboration reaches its first commercial pilot milestone, it would also surface here, though the five-year, $100-million-each framework deliberately defers near-term revenue expectations.

**The C-DAC delivery (H2 2026, specific quarter unconfirmed)** is the dominant catalyst of the entire twelve-month window. The $8.4 million contract is the company's largest single hardware order on record and its first substantial deployment outside NATO-aligned markets. Hardware delivery in Rigetti's contract structure triggers formal revenue recognition, meaning that whichever quarter the 108-qubit Cepheus-class system arrives at C-DAC's facility in India becomes, by definition, Rigetti's highest-revenue quarter since inception. Execution risk is real: the Cepheus-1-108Q only reached general availability ~~in Q1 2026~~ ==on April 7, 2026==, meaning C-DAC will receive a system built on architecture with less than two quarters of production history.

**The DOC LOI conversion (timing uncertain, potentially Q3 or Q4 2026)** is the highest-optionality item on the calendar. The letter of intent ~~signed in March 2026~~ ==announced May 21, 2026== for up to $100 million in R&D funding under national quantum computing programs has no confirmed award date in disclosed materials. DOC grant conversion timelines under U.S. domestic technology investment programs have historically ranged from six to eighteen months from LOI to binding contract. If a substantive tranche is awarded before year-end 2026, it would transform Rigetti's revenue profile and add to a cash balance that is already sufficient for a ~~four-plus-year~~ ==nine-plus-year== runway.

**Q3 2026 earnings (expected early November 2026)** will either confirm or deny the C-DAC revenue recognition has occurred. Analysts will also watch for any announced expansion of the UK deployment: the company's stated plan to invest up to ~~£100 million~~ ==US$100 million== in the United Kingdom over three to four years for a greater-than-1,000-qubit system implies that engineering and site preparation work should be visible in either capital spending disclosures or UK corporate filings by late 2026.

**Q4 2026 and the full-year 2026 print (expected early March 2027)** will close the fiscal year and serve as the first comparison against what will almost certainly be disclosed formal revenue guidance — if the company follows the IonQ model of introducing annual guidance only after its commercial pipeline achieves a minimum threshold of predictability.

## What Consensus Expects

Rigetti's sell-side coverage is sparse by the standards of an $8.79 billion market-capitalization company. The speculative sector dynamics and small float of institutional-quality shares constrain the analyst base, meaning published consensus estimates carry wider-than-normal dispersion. Based on the disclosed contract pipeline — C-DAC at $8.4 million, Novera backlog, the Quanta collaboration's initial phases, and cloud QCS subscriptions — implied full-year 2026 revenue sits in a range of approximately $18 million to $28 million, representing growth of 155 percent to 295 percent from FY2025's $7.1 million. The midpoint of that range, roughly $23 million, would represent the company's highest annual revenue figure since inception and first year in which hardware delivery (rather than technology-development grants) would constitute the majority of the top line.

| Period | Implied Revenue Range | YoY Growth (midpoint) | Non-GAAP Op. Loss (est.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026 | $3.0M – $5.5M | flat to modest sequential | ~$14M – $16M |
| Q3 2026 | $5.0M – $10.0M | significant (C-DAC timing) | ~$14M – $16M |
| Q4 2026 | $4.0M – $8.0M | high vs. Q4 2025 ($1.6M) | ~$14M – $16M |
| FY2026 | $18.0M – $28.0M | 155% – 295% vs. $7.1M | ~$55M – $65M |

Non-GAAP operating losses are expected to remain roughly flat quarter-over-quarter in the $14 million to $16 million range, reflecting the cost base associated with operating Fab-1, scaling the Quanta collaboration, and sustaining engineering headcount. The structural cash burn of $12 to $15 million per quarter per management's implied guidance leaves the $569 million balance largely intact through the forecast window, barring a major acceleration of capital expenditure for the UK facility.

## Management's Signposts

Rigetti does not issue formal financial guidance in the conventional semiconductor sense. On the Q1 2026 earnings call — the most recent reference point in the frozen window — management's forward commentary was framed around hardware delivery and partnership milestones rather than revenue ranges. The C-DAC delivery commitment of H2 2026 is the closest thing to a hard forward promise in the public record. Management has also confirmed that the Quanta partnership is moving from planning into early commercial execution, with joint go-to-market activity for Cepheus-class systems at hyperscale and national-lab customers scheduled to begin in 2026. The DOC LOI was characterized as part of Rigetti's broader positioning in the U.S. government's quantum technology investment program, with no specific timing guidance on award.

## Metrics That Matter Each Quarter

Four numbers carry most of the thesis-testing weight. **Revenue per quarter**, broken down between hardware delivery and cloud access, determines whether the commercialization inflection is compound or one-time. Any quarter in which hardware revenue exceeds cloud revenue for the first time would mark a structural milestone. **Non-GAAP operating loss per quarter** confirms whether cost discipline is holding during the Quanta scale-up — a loss materially above $16 million would suggest investment acceleration that demands explanation. **Qubit count and fidelity progress disclosures** in earnings presentations serve as the technical credibility signal: the progression from ~~99.5%~~ ==99.1%== median fidelity (Cepheus-1 at launch) toward the 99.9% figure demonstrated on the prototype is the roadmap marker that underpins the 1,000-qubit UK system narrative. Finally, **new contract announcements**, specifically any enterprise or hyperscale cloud award enabled by the Quanta distribution network, would constitute the first evidence that Rigetti's commercial model extends beyond government procurement.

## Beat, Miss, and the Margin of Surprise

A beat in the next twelve months most likely originates from one of two sources: an accelerated C-DAC delivery that pulls $8.4 million revenue recognition from Q3 into Q2, or a DOC contract award that adds a material revenue tranche before year-end. Either event would push FY2026 revenue to the upper end of the $18 million to $28 million range and likely re-rate the stock against its peers. An upside surprise from the Quanta partnership — say, an announced order for multiple Cepheus-class systems from a named hyperscale customer — would be orders of magnitude more significant than any government hardware delivery in terms of market reaction, because it would validate the commercial sales model that the entire valuation thesis requires.

A miss most likely originates from C-DAC delivery slippage beyond 2026 into 2027 — either due to hardware yield problems at Fab-1, integration delays at the customer site, or export control complications in the India channel. A one-quarter slip would reduce FY2026 revenue by approximately thirty percent at the midpoint. A two-quarter slip into early 2027 would push full-year 2026 revenue back toward the FY2025 baseline and would require management to explain why the Cepheus-class production process has not met its own publicly committed timeline.

## Bull and Bear: The Asymmetry at the Frozen Snapshot

The bull case is a sequential stack of binary catalysts: C-DAC delivers on schedule, the DOC LOI converts, the Quanta channel secures one named enterprise customer, and the UK 1,000-qubit facility moves from announcement to groundbreaking. None of these is improbable individually, and if two or three arrive in the same fiscal year, consensus revenue revisions would be sharp — the base is low enough that any material new contract registers as a double-digit percentage move on the forward multiple. The cash cushion eliminates financing risk through the entire scenario, meaning the bull case is pure execution optionality priced on a $589 million war chest.

The bear case is simpler and just as plausible: hardware at 108 qubits is not yet practically useful enough to justify recurring enterprise spending, C-DAC and the NQCC deployments remain isolated government pilots rather than the first nodes of a replicable network, and the 1,000-qubit threshold — the commercially meaningful system size — is still two to three hardware generations away. In that scenario, FY2026 revenue lands at $15 to $20 million and the $8.79 billion market capitalization continues to price a 2029-2031 payoff that may or may not materialize before capital markets lose patience.

The asymmetry, as it stands at the frozen snapshot, is characteristic of deep-technology options: downside is bounded by the balance sheet (the company does not need to raise capital to survive), while upside is bounded only by how quickly practical quantum advantage materializes and how much of that value Rigetti's vertical integration allows it to capture.

chapters.title: 2026-2030 Horizon: Toward Practical Quantum Advantage, the 1,000-Qubit Milestone, and Commercial Break-Even
chapters.body:
## The 2026 Revenue Conversion: Three Catalysts and a Proof-of-Concept Year

Rigetti Computing entered 2026 carrying something it had not possessed in the four years since its SPAC listing: a hardware order backlog with delivery dates. The $8.4 million purchase order from India's Centre for Development of Advanced Computing, secured in late 2025 for a 108-qubit Cepheus-class on-premises system scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2026, represented the company's largest single hardware contract and the first meaningful test of whether engineering milestones could convert into quarterly revenue recognition on a predictable timeline.

The revenue arithmetic for FY2026 turns on three variables. First, the C-DAC system: assuming delivery against the purchase order in Q3 or Q4 2026, the contract's $8.4 million would likely be recognized on an installation-and-acceptance basis, potentially doubling Rigetti's full-year revenue relative to the $7.1 million [reported for FY2025](https://investors.rigetti.com/news-releases/news-release-details/rigetti-computing-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-yvxoh4p8fn7k). Q1 2026 alone delivered $4.4 million — 193 percent year-over-year growth — driven ~~by partial Cepheus milestone billing and Novera QPU shipments~~ ==mainly by higher Novera system and related product sales, including the University of Saskatchewan shipment==. If the run rate holds, FY2026 revenue of $15 million to $20 million is plausible; the C-DAC delivery alone could push the range to $20 million or beyond. Second, the Department of Commerce letter of intent ~~signed in March 2026~~ ==announced May 21, 2026== for up to $100 million in R&D funding: LOI-stage government agreements do not generate revenue until formal grant awards are executed, a process that in U.S. federal procurement typically spans six to eighteen months, meaning meaningful DOC dollars are unlikely to appear before late 2026 at earliest and more probably in 2027. Third, the Novera QPU pipeline: the Japanese research institution delivery expected in April 2026, combined with additional government lab targets across the partner program, could contribute incremental millions if two or three additional units ship during the year.

The honest FY2026 revenue projection, based on disclosed contracts, sits in the $15 million to $25 million range — a material step up from $7.1 million but still a fraction of what the $8.79 billion market capitalization implies about the company's long-run potential. FY2026 is best characterized as a proof-of-concept year for hardware commercialization, not a commercialization inflection.

## The 1,000-Qubit Roadmap: What Must Be Demonstrated Versus What Has Been Stated

Rigetti's announcement in March 2026 that it would invest up to $100 million in the United Kingdom over three to four years to deploy a greater-than-1,000-qubit system placed a timestamp on the company's most ambitious technical commitment. The implication is a 1,000-qubit system by 2029 or 2030 — a timeline that requires executing on several technically distinct problems simultaneously.

The Cepheus-1-108Q chiplet architecture, ~~launched in general availability in Q1 2026~~ ==which entered general availability on April 7, 2026==, has demonstrated ~~99.5 percent median fidelity using fSim gates~~ ==99.1 percent current median two-qubit gate fidelity at general availability, with 99.5 percent set as a later-2026 target==, and a prototype at 28-nanosecond gate speed achieved 99.9 percent two-qubit gate fidelity. These figures approach the threshold theoretically required for meaningful near-term error correction experiments. The chiplet approach — connecting multiple smaller processors rather than fabricating a single monolithic wafer — is the correct engineering strategy for scaling toward 1,000 qubits; no organization has been able to maintain competitive fidelity on monolithic superconducting chips beyond approximately 100 qubits.

What Rigetti has demonstrated is: chiplet-based modular architecture at 108 qubits with competitive fidelity. What it has stated but not yet shown at scale is: cryogenic inter-chip connectivity at 200-to-500-qubit-per-chiplet yield, real-time classical control overhead capable of handling the error syndromes generated by 1,000-qubit operation without collapsing coherence times, and fabrication throughput at Fab-1 in Fremont sufficient to produce chiplets with consistent yield at that scale. Each step requires compounding fidelity improvements; errors that are manageable at 108 qubits become catastrophic at 1,000 without fault-tolerant correction overhead running in parallel.

The intermediate 2027-2028 period is therefore primarily a fabrication and cryogenics engineering challenge. IBM's 2025-era roadmap has shown publicly that scaling modular superconducting systems confronts diminishing returns in coherence time per additional qubit — a problem Rigetti will face regardless of architectural choices. The UK deployment commitment, backed by the government's £2 billion national quantum program, provides both funding and a credibility anchor, but it also creates reputational risk if fidelity targets at scale slip.

## The Quanta Variable: Distribution Partner or Revenue Game-Changer?

The February 2025 strategic collaboration with Quanta Computer introduced a variable that changes the commercial calculus more than any government contract. Quanta, with approximately $43 billion in annual revenue, is the world's leading server and notebook manufacturer — its global distribution network reaches hyperscale data center operators, cloud providers, and government technology programs across Asia, North America, and Europe. If Quanta's enterprise relationships bring a single hyperscale cloud provider or major government agency to a multi-unit Rigetti QPU procurement, the revenue impact would be transformational.

| Scenario | Units | Average Contract Value | Annual Revenue Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single government lab (Novera-class) | 3-5 | $0.5–1M | $1.5–5M |
| Mid-tier enterprise (Cepheus-class) | 2–3 | $8–12M | $16–36M |
| Hyperscale/data center (next-gen system) | 5–10 | $15–25M | $75–250M |

The bear case for the Quanta partnership is equally concrete. Taiwan's geopolitical exposure — Quanta's headquarters and primary manufacturing are in Taipei — creates supply chain and partnership continuity risk in scenarios involving U.S.-China-Taiwan tensions. Joint intellectual property questions around co-developed quantum-classical integration stacks have not been disclosed in detail; if Quanta's manufacturing contributions generate IP claims on Rigetti's QPU architectures, future licensing arrangements could constrain Rigetti's margins. The partnership's five-year, $100-million-each commitment also means that meaningful distribution impact is unlikely to appear before 2027, making 2026 a relationship-building year rather than a revenue year for this channel.

## The 2028-2030 Practical Advantage Window

The industries most likely to demonstrate first commercial quantum advantage — drug discovery and molecular simulation, financial portfolio optimization, logistics, and cryptographic key management — share a common profile: they involve optimization over enormous combinatorial spaces that scale exponentially for classical computers but polynomially for fault-tolerant quantum systems.
